title: The Ministry Bibliographer and the Initiation Beneath the Sphinx: Jean-Baptiste Pitois, called Paul Christian
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Remiremont to La Trappe: the Boy Called Marie-Bernard

stops.name: Remiremont, birth in the Vosges
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF authority record and the encyclopedia.com biographical entry independently give 15 May 1811 at Remiremont, Vosges. The coordinate is the town center: no house, street, or parish within the town is established.
stops.campa: Jean Baptiste Pitois is born at Remiremont, a small town of the Vosges under wooded hills, in a family whose records name no father and whose wider connections include a bookseller-publisher, Pitois-Levrault. Paper is already the family trade at one remove. The household destines the boy for the priesthood before he can be asked about it, and the two houses he will spend fifty years moving between, the Church and the printing shop, are both waiting for him in the year he is born. The register gives 15 May 1811.
suggested_refs: The parish and civil registers of Remiremont, Vosges, for May 1811
sources: La litterature francaise contemporaine, on the bookseller-publisher Pitois-Levrault (via secondary synthesis)

stops.name: Harcourt, the church school
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; reported by Ross Nichols and repeated across tarot-history literature, with no school register, parish record, or bill of board located. The year is an ordering approximation within the early 1820s and the month and day are placeholders. Coordinate corrected to the commune of Harcourt, Eure, per fr.wikipedia.
stops.campa: Under local ecclesiastical supervision the boy is set to Latin and catechism at a church school at Harcourt in Normandy, the first stage of an education his family has planned to its end. From there the schooling is said to continue in Paris among the Clercs de la Chapelle Royale, nearer the altar and nearer the court. No register, no roll, no bill for his board survives for either house. Everything anyone knows about these years comes from a biography assembled after his death, out of what his son remembered being told.
suggested_refs: The Benedictine and parish school buildings of Harcourt, Eure
Ross Nichols's biographical introduction to The History and Practice of Magic
sources: Ross Nichols, biographical reconstruction, as summarized in modern tarot-history scholarship

stops.name: Soligny-la-Trappe, the novice takes the name Marie-Bernard
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the novitiate at La Trappe and the religious name Marie-Bernard are reported across the occult-tarot biographies, with no monastic record located and no source naming the specific house. Encyclopedia.com independently confirms only that he was raised in a monastic community by a family who wanted him in the priesthood. Month and day are placeholders. The coordinate is the abbey itself, which had resettled at Soligny in 1827 and so was an active Trappist house in 1828.
stops.campa: At about seventeen he enters Notre-Dame de la Grande Trappe, resettled at Soligny only a year earlier, and takes the religious name Marie-Bernard. Silence, the night office, the abbey's ground worked by hand: he keeps the rule for roughly a year and leaves without permanent vows. The name stays with him. He gives it to his son. In 1855 he puts six volumes of Catholic history under the authorship of an aged monk called Dom Marie-Bernard, and there is no such monk.
suggested_refs: The Abbaye Notre-Dame de la Trappe at Soligny-la-Trappe, Orne, resettled 1827
sources: Secondary occult-tarot biographies summarizing the La Trappe episode
fr.wikipedia, 'Abbaye Notre-Dame de la Trappe', for the coordinate and the 1827 resettlement

stops.name: Strasbourg, the uncle's academy
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Ross Nichols reports an uncle holding the rectorship of the academy and further study at Strasbourg. No university register, matriculation, thesis, or qualification was located anywhere. Year approximate, month and day placeholders.
stops.campa: Out of the cloister and east to the Rhine, where an uncle is said to hold the rectorship of the academy and to take the former novice in. He studies. Nothing says what. No faculty list carries his name, no thesis, no certificate, no matriculation. The only trace these years leave is in the work that follows: German good enough to render Hoffmann and Christoph von Schmid into French for Paris publishers through the 1840s. He is eighteen when he arrives. Nothing records when he leaves.
suggested_refs: The registers of the Academie de Strasbourg for the late 1820s
sources: Ross Nichols, as reported in secondary tarot-history sources

stops.name: Fort-de-France, the abolitionist legend
stops.date_confidence: tradition; traced to a posthumous biographical serial in the journal La Lumiere (1893-1894), apparently furnished by Pitois's son, and retold by every later occult biographer. No ship's list, passport, consular note, police report, or newspaper account was located. The date is an ordering placeholder inside an undated early 1830s.
stops.campa: The family tradition sends the young man across the Atlantic to Martinique and into agitation against slavery, and on from there to Spain to fight beside partisans. Slavery is legal in the French islands and will remain so until 1848. The story reaches print in 1893, sixteen years after his death, in a serial his own son appears to have furnished, and every biographer since has repeated it. No ship's list, no consular note, no police report and no newspaper puts Pitois on Martinique in any year.
suggested_refs: The biographical serial on Pitois in La Lumiere, 1893-1894
sources: La Lumiere serial (1893-1894), via modern tarot-historical scholarship; the serial itself was not located in this pass

stops.name: Roseau, the same legend on a different island
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and internally contradictory; Ross Nichols's retelling names Dominica where other versions of the same story name Martinique. Dominica was a British possession, which sits badly with the French colonial framing of the tale and suggests transmission error rather than a second episode. Date is a placeholder.
stops.campa: A second version of the same adventure sets him down at Dominica, an island held by the British crown, which nothing in the tale accounts for. Two islands, one anecdote, and not a document under either of them. Ross Nichols tells it with Dominica; the family serial of 1893 tells it with Martinique. Neither version is dropped and neither is preferred. The tale travelled by mouth through a family for two generations before anyone set it in type. Which harbour, if either, the young man actually saw, nothing answers.
suggested_refs: Roseau harbour, Dominica, under British administration in the 1830s
sources: Ross Nichols's retelling, per the dossier; uncorroborated

stops.name: Paris, the Revue Germanique
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; modern tarot historians place him at the Revue Germanique in these years, but no masthead or archival record naming him was located. His presence in Parisian literary journalism in the later 1830s is separately supported by encyclopedia.com and by the BnF authority record. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: By the middle thirties he is inside Parisian literary journalism, attached to the Revue Germanique, the natural desk for a man who reads German and will translate it for money for the next decade. The pay is by the line and the work is unsigned. Tarot historians reconstruct this posting from later accounts; no masthead names him. What the record does support is his presence in Parisian literary journalism through these years. He is in his twenties, a provincial without patrimony, living off periodicals.
suggested_refs: Surviving runs of the Revue Germanique, 1836-1838

stops.name: Paris, L'Eclair and the Gazette des salons
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; both posts come down through the same secondary tarot-history literature, repeating one another, with no masthead confirmed by direct fetch in this pass. L'Eclair is dated 1838 and the Gazette des salons 1839-1840 in those accounts. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He moves through two more papers, L'Eclair and then the Gazette des salons, the ordinary itinerary of a man taking whatever a desk pays. It is the exact interval in which he attaches himself to Charles Nodier and to the Arsenal, and in which he begins the translating that will run to a hundred catalogue entries. The three periodical posts come down through reconstruction, one historian citing the last. Not one of them can be confirmed from a masthead.
suggested_refs: Eugene Hatin's bibliography of the French periodical press

stops.name: Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal, Nodier's circle and Paris historique
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF authority record states that he collaborated with Charles Nodier at the Arsenal library, and encyclopedia.com independently confirms the association and lists Paris historique among his works, dated 1838-1839. The record supports collaboration, not a staff post; later occult biography inflates it into an apprenticeship. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Charles Nodier keeps the Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal and holds a salon inside it, and Pitois enters the circle. Out of the association comes Paris historique, promenade dans les rues de Paris, a lavish illustrated work with plates by Auguste Regnier and Champin, for which Pitois writes the whole historical resume. Pitois is twenty-seven. The national library's authority record states the collaboration and does not divide the labour. On the spine and on the title page stands one name, Nodier's.
suggested_refs: Paris historique, promenade dans les rues de Paris (1838-1839), with plates by Auguste Regnier and Champin
The reading room of the Bibliotheque de l'Arsenal under Nodier's librarianship
sources: onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu, author listing for Pitois, Christian, 1811-1877

stops.name: Paris, the library of the Ministry of Public Instruction
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF authority record describes him as attached to the library of the Ministry of Public Instruction and encyclopedia.com independently gives the 1839 appointment. The coordinate is approximate: the ministry's 1839 premises are not established. The inventory work on confiscated monastic libraries, and the discovery of astrological books in it, are his own later account of himself. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He is appointed to the library of the Ministry of Public Instruction, work that means inventories: duplicate copies to be listed, and the volumes swept up from monastic libraries confiscated fifty years earlier still waiting to be sorted. He will say later that this is where he first opened the old books of astrology and Egyptian mystery that made him what he became. Two independent records confirm the appointment. For the scene of discovery the only witness is Christian himself, writing of it thirty years on.
suggested_refs: The confiscated monastic collections of the Revolution, still uncatalogued in the ministry depots of the 1830s

stops.name: Paris, the translation years
stops.date_confidence: attested by catalogue, with the older account corrected: BnF search returns Montaigne's Essais (1842), the Poemes gaeliques of Ossian (1842), Young's Nuits (1842), Helvetius's De l'Esprit with a prefatory essay (1843), Washington Irving's L'Alhambra (1843), Hoffmann's Contes fantastiques (1843), Boccaccio's Decameron (1844) and Christoph von Schmid titles from 1839 to 1846. Machiavelli, named in older accounts of his output, appears nowhere among the roughly one hundred BnF records under his authority and is dropped here.
stops.campa: For eight years he translates and adapts on an industrial scale: Montaigne and Young and the Ossian poems in 1842, Helvetius with a prefatory essay of his own and Washington Irving's Alhambra and Hoffmann's Contes fantastiques in 1843, Boccaccio's Decameron in 1844, and the pious tales of Christoph von Schmid running from 1839 to 1846, some issued under the imprint form Christian Pitois-Levrault. Older accounts of his output add Machiavelli to the list. No such record exists in the hundred the national library holds under his name.
suggested_refs: The BnF authority file's roughly one hundred records under Christian, P. (Pitois, Jean-Baptiste)

stops.name: Algiers, secretary to Marshal Bugeaud
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF authority record calls him private secretary to Marshal Bugeaud, encyclopedia.com gives service in Algiers in 1843-1844, and Bonnie Effros, Incidental Archaeologists (Cornell, 2018), independently identifies him as a Ministry of Public Instruction bibliographer serving as Bugeaud's personal secretary. Algiers stands for the theater; no single address or posting within Algeria is documented. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The bibliographer of the Ministry crosses the sea as private secretary to Marshal Thomas-Robert Bugeaud, governor-general, and writes at the elbow of the razzia: columns sent out to burn standing grain and drive off herds until the tribes submit. The war is against Emir Abdelkader, whose mobile capital of some thirty thousand people is taken in May of Pitois's first African year. Pitois holds no rank and does not fight. He is there to keep the marshal's correspondence, and he stays about two years.
suggested_refs: The French military headquarters in the Casbah of Algiers under Bugeaud's governorship
sources: Bonnie Effros, Incidental Archaeologists (Cornell University Press, 2018)
abdelkader.journey.json, for the dates of the razzia campaign and the taking of the smala

stops.name: The Djurdjura, the quicksand and the pistol
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the episode comes through the posthumous family account said to draw on a diary, with no military report, correspondence, or contemporary newspaper located. The Kabylia coordinate is a marker for an unspecified site, not an identified one. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The family account has him caught in quicksand in the Kabyle country, sunk to the chest, a fighter standing over him with a blade at his neck; his pistol, which he knows to be unloaded, goes off; a French detachment reaches him; he comes out of it with two bullet wounds in him. The account is said to rest on a diary. No diary has been produced, and no military report, letter or newspaper notice has been found to set beside it. His service in Algeria is documented twice over; the afternoon in the quicksand survives only in his son's telling.
suggested_refs: The Djurdjura range of Kabylia, theatre of the 1844 French columns
sources: Posthumous family tradition via La Lumiere (1893-1894) and Ross Nichols; no independent record found

stops.name: Paris, Souvenir du marechal Bugeaud
stops.date_confidence: attested as a publication by the BnF and UPenn bibliographic listings, dated 1845. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Back at a Paris desk he turns the African year into Souvenir du marechal Bugeaud, de l'Algerie et du Maroc, the first of four books he draws from a posting that lasted barely two. The marshal is a national figure and the conquest sells. Pitois writes it as a chronicler with access, which he genuinely had, and the book does for him what such books do for a man of letters with no capital: it makes his name worth a contract. The Algerian material will carry him to 1847.
suggested_refs: Souvenir du marechal Bugeaud, de l'Algerie et du Maroc (Paris, 1845)
sources: BnF catalogue records under his authority

stops.name: Paris, L'Afrique francaise and the caves of the Dahra
stops.date_confidence: the publication is attested (UPenn Online Books dates L'Afrique francaise to 1846). That the book transmits testimony on the Dahra asphyxiations and can be critical of French pacification is reported by Bonnie Effros and was not re-verified against the volume in this pass. Pitois was not in Africa in June 1845; the testimony reaches him second hand. The Dahra cave itself is not his stop and is cited here as a reference. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: In June 1845 Colonel Pelissier's column drives the Ouled Riah into the cave of Ghar el-Frechih in the Dahra massif and lights fires at every mouth of it for two days. More than a thousand people die inside the rock. Pitois, a year off the marshal's staff, prints testimony about it in Paris in L'Afrique francaise, l'empire de Maroc et les deserts de Sahara, and his handling of the pacification can be sharp. He had left Africa the year before and takes the account from men who were at the cave mouth. The book appears in 1846.
suggested_refs: The Ghar el-Frechih cave at Nekmaria in the Dahra, sealed by fire 18-20 June 1845
Bonnie Effros, Incidental Archaeologists, on Pitois as a critical chronicler of the conquest
sources: Bonnie Effros, Incidental Archaeologists (Cornell University Press, 2018)
abdelkader.journey.json, for the Nekmaria stop dated 1845-06-19

stops.name: Paris, L'Algerie de la jeunesse
stops.date_confidence: attested as a publication in the UPenn bibliographic listing, dated 1847. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The last of the African books puts the conquest into a form fit for schoolboys: L'Algerie de la jeunesse, 1847. The razzia, the smala, the submission of the tribes, arranged as instruction for the young of the metropolis. He is thirty-six, employed by the Ministry of Public Instruction, and writing the empire's account of itself for the classroom. Nothing he has printed in twenty years suggests any quarrel with the regime that pays him. Within a year the monarchy that ordered the conquest will fall in three February days.
suggested_refs: L'Algerie de la jeunesse (Paris, 1847)

stops.name: Paris, the opening session of the Club central des Jacobins
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF catalogue holds the printed pamphlet 'Club central des Jacobins. Discours prononce a la seance d'ouverture, le 29 mars 1848' under his authority, which is documentary evidence independent of Maitron, whose pages returned 403 Forbidden on two fetch attempts. The meeting hall is genuinely unlocated; the coordinate is a Palais-Royal district placeholder, that quarter being a common venue for the clubs of 1848.
stops.campa: Five weeks after the February revolution, in a hall the record does not locate, the opening session of the Club central des Jacobins is called to order by its provisional president, styled on the printed pamphlet as le citoyen Pitois, Christian. The man who spent the previous decade translating devotional tales and writing the conquest of Algeria for children stands up and claims the inheritance of 1793 by name. The speech is printed as a pamphlet, Discours prononce a la seance d'ouverture, le 29 mars 1848, and catalogued under his authority at the national library.
suggested_refs: The printed pamphlet of the opening address, Club central des Jacobins, 29 March 1848, BnF
sources: Maitron, maitron.fr, entry on Pitois-Christian, Jean-Baptiste: inaccessible, 403 Forbidden on two attempts

stops.name: Paris, the Journal des Jacobins, one issue
stops.date_confidence: the periodical is attested: BnF holds 'Journal des Jacobins: sentinelle des droits de l'homme' (1848) under his authority. That it ran to a single issue, and that he was its editor-in-chief, come from Eugene Hatin's nineteenth-century press bibliography by way of a rare-book description, not fetched in this pass. The office address is unknown and the month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: The club gets a paper: Journal des Jacobins, sentinelle des droits de l'homme, with Pitois-Christian at the head of it. The national library holds it under his authority. By the account of Eugene Hatin, who catalogued the press of the century, it ran to a single issue and stopped. The spring of 1848 produces hundreds of such papers. Where the office stood, who set the type and what the single number carried are all unestablished; no copy has been described in print.
suggested_refs: Eugene Hatin, Bibliographie historique et critique de la presse periodique francaise
sources: Hatin via a rare-book bibliographic description; not independently fetched

stops.name: Paris, the order of 23 June and the arrest of 31 July
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; both dates come from the Maitron biographical dictionary, whose pages returned 403 Forbidden on two fetch attempts and could not be read directly for this file. No charge, court judgment, or conviction is claimed even in that account. His home address in Paris is not established and the coordinate is the canonical Paris pin.
stops.campa: On 23 June, the day the barricades go up in the eastern faubourgs and Cavaignac is handed the city, an executive order for Pitois's arrest is issued. The arrest itself waits five weeks and comes on 31 July, with papers seized at his home and treated as incriminating. No charge is named in the account that survives, no trial, no judgment. Both dates come from a single biographical dictionary of the labour movement, whose pages refused every request made to them.
stops.quote: The Sphinx, balanced on the top of this wheel, holds a sword in its lion's paws. It personifies Destiny ever ready to strike left or right; according to the direction in which it turns the wheel the humblest rises and the highest is cast down.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), Arcanum X: The Sphinx, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw, written twenty-two years after the arrest
suggested_refs: The June Days of 1848 and the repression under Cavaignac
sources: Maitron, maitron.fr, entry on Pitois-Christian, Jean-Baptiste: inaccessible, 403 Forbidden

stops.name: Paris, transported to a place the record does not name
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and incomplete; Maitron reports that he was transporte, and no source reachable in this pass names the destination, the sentence, or the conditions. Belle-Ile-en-Mer and Algeria are documented destinations for the 1848 transportes as a class, never for Pitois by name. The stop is pinned at the point of departure because the point of arrival has no name in any source consulted. Month is a placeholder.
stops.campa: He is transported. The word is nearly all the record gives: transporte, a sentence carried out on thousands after the June Days, to the hulks, to Belle-Ile, to Algeria, to wherever the Republic had room for them. Which of these took Pitois is written nowhere that can be reached. The departure from Paris is the last point at which his track can be fixed; the destination has no name in any source consulted. He is thirty-seven and has published perhaps forty volumes.
suggested_refs: The transportation sentences following the June Days, 1848
sources: Maitron, maitron.fr: inaccessible, 403 Forbidden on two attempts

stops.name: Paris, pardoned and returned
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; Maitron gives the pardon and a return from transportation in December 1849, and Maitron could not be fetched. The day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Pardoned, he comes back to Paris in December 1849, after a punishment whose length, place, and conditions are all unrecorded. Nothing is known of what it did to him except what he prints next, and what he prints next is a book on the agony of the Revolution, written against the thing he stood up for in March 1848. Between the Jacobin platform and that title lie seventeen months and one arrest. The Second Republic that arrested him is still standing, with Louis-Napoleon at its head.
suggested_refs: Dieu et France. Agonie de la Revolution (Paris, 1850)

segments.name: The Recantation and the Invented Monk

stops.name: Paris, Dieu et France and the evening paper
stops.date_confidence: the 1850 title is attested in bibliography; the Moniteur du Soir staff post, dated roughly 1850-1852, is a reconstruction from tarot-history scholarship with no masthead located. The coordinate is the central Paris press quarter, not a documented office. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: In 1850 he publishes Dieu et France. Agonie de la Revolution. God and France, in that order, from the citizen-president of the Jacobin club, ten months out of transportation. Whether that is conviction, exhaustion, or the price of working in a Paris where a coup is being prepared, the record does not say and he never explains it. He is thirty-nine, and he has been a Trappist novice, a translator, a colonial chronicler, a Jacobin and a convict. He takes a place on the staff of the Moniteur du Soir and stays about two years.
suggested_refs: Dieu et France. Agonie de la Revolution (Paris, 1850)
sources: Modern tarot-history scholarship and Ross Nichols, for the Moniteur du Soir years

stops.name: Paris, the Italian wife said to be a Scott
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and contradicted, and not resolved here; Maitron reports a marriage in 1853 to an Italian woman said to be related to Walter Scott, with no marriage act located and Maitron itself inaccessible (403). Against it stands a Lyon civil-register index giving his marriage to Louise Marie Tortillet on 26 June 1877. Neither is confirmed and neither is dropped. The place of the 1853 marriage is unspecified in the source; the stop is pinned at Paris, where he was living.
stops.campa: A marriage is reported for this year, to an Italian woman said to be related to Walter Scott. The act has not been found. Against it stands a Lyon civil register giving his marriage to Louise Marie Tortillet in June 1877, sixteen days before his death, and there is no reconciling the two without a document that neither source produces. Both are set down and neither is chosen. Whether he married once, twice, or in neither of those years is not a thing the registers now reachable will settle.
suggested_refs: The Paris and Lyon marriage registers for 1853 and 1877
sources: gw.geneanet.org/jfriedel, citing 'Mariages de Lyon 02': inaccessible, 403 Forbidden

stops.name: Paris, Histoire de la Terreur
stops.date_confidence: attested as a publication in the UPenn and BnF listings, dated 1853. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Five years after his own arrest, and one year after the Empire is proclaimed, he publishes Histoire de la Terreur. The Jacobin who presided in March 1848 writes the history of the Jacobins who governed in 1793, under a censorship that would not have let him admire them. He is producing two and three volumes a year now, on any subject a publisher will buy. Whether the book leans toward the men of 1793 or against them, nobody has yet read it against his own speech to find out.
suggested_refs: Histoire de la Terreur (Paris, 1853)

stops.name: The Tuileries, a prophecy dated backward
stops.date_confidence: the publication is attested: 'Carmen sybillinum. 3 avril 1854' goes to print in 1856, after the Crimean victory and the birth of the imperial heir it claims to foresee. The 1854 dating, and the acknowledgment said to come from an official of the Empress's household, are the work's own self-presentation and rest on no independently dated pre-event record.
stops.campa: He composes a prophecy and dates it 3 April 1854: French arms will triumph in the Crimea, and an heir will be born to the imperial house. Both come to pass. Sebastopol falls in September 1855 and the Prince Imperial is born in March 1856, and only then does the poem go to a printer. An acknowledgment from an official of the Empress's household is claimed for the piece. No copy dated before those events has been found, and the 1854 heading is carried by the 1856 printing alone. It appears from the Bureau de l'Echo des feuilletons.
suggested_refs: Carmen sybillinum. 3 avril 1854 (Bureau de l'Echo des feuilletons, 1856)
sources: Publication record of the 1856 printing, per modern tarot-historical scholarship; the pamphlet itself was not fetched in this pass

stops.name: Paris, Dom Marie-Bernard writes Les Heros du christianisme
stops.date_confidence: the series is attested in bibliography, dated from 1855; the invented monastic authorship and Christian's later public disclosure that he wrote the whole of it are reported in Decker, Depaulis and Dummett and the literature descending from them, and were not verified in this pass against the volumes' front matter. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Les Heros du christianisme appears under the authorship of Dom Marie-Bernard, an aged monk, with Christian named on the title page only as its editor and annotator. There is no such monk. The name is the one Pitois took as a novice at La Trappe at seventeen, handed back to a fictional man of the cloth in order to sell Catholic history by the volume. He disclosed the invention publicly some years later, and said that he had written every page of the series himself.
suggested_refs: Les Heros du christianisme, published as by Dom Marie-Bernard, Paris, from 1855
sources: Ronald Decker, Thierry Depaulis and Michael Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards (Duckworth, 1996), and the secondary literature descending from it
Bibliographic record of the series title

stops.name: Paris, seven sacraments, seven novels
stops.date_confidence: attested by catalogue, with the older single date corrected: BnF records give Les Coeurs brises (penance), L'Echo des Catacombes (confirmation) and La Prison mamertine (baptism) in 1859, and L'Ange de Wehrda (marriage), La Crosse et le glaive (ordination), La Foret vierge (extreme unction), Une page de ma vie (the Eucharist) and Les Fleurs du ciel in 1860. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Seven novels, one sacrament each, across two years: Les Coeurs brises for penance, L'Echo des Catacombes for confirmation, La Prison mamertine for baptism, then in 1860 L'Ange de Wehrda for marriage, La Crosse et le glaive for ordination, La Foret vierge for extreme unction, Une page de ma vie for the Eucharist, with Les Fleurs du ciel over them all. A closed set of mysteries, numbered, each with its emblem and its story. Three years later he does it again with twenty-two.
suggested_refs: The seven sacrament novels of 1859-1860, each subtitled with its sacrament

segments.name: The Red Man of the Tuileries

stops.name: Paris, 22 rue d'Angouleme: the seventy-eight houses
stops.date_confidence: the 1863 publication is attested in bibliography and analysed by Decker, Depaulis and Dummett; the title-page address, 22 rue d'Angouleme by the Champs-Elysees, comes through the dossier's reading of that title page, and a direct fetch of a scanned copy returned only upload metadata. The street has since been renamed, so the coordinate is an approximation within the quarter. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He publishes L'Homme rouge des Tuileries himself and prints his own address on the title page: 22 rue d'Angouleme, by the Champs-Elysees. The red man is the specter Paris held to have appeared to Napoleon Bonaparte before the fall, and Christian builds his first public occult system around it, advertised as illustrated with twenty-two kabbalistic figures. Inside, the seventy-eight cards of the tarot are rebuilt as symbolic houses and the trumps are renamed: the Magus, Isis-Urania, the Sphinx, Typhon, the Crocodile at zero.
stops.quote: Arcanum 0 represents the punishment following every error. You can see here a blind man carrying a full beggar's wallet about to collide with a broken obelisk, on which a crocodile is waiting with open jaws.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), Arcanum 0: The Crocodile, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw; the trump was numbered zero already in the 1863 system
suggested_refs: L'Homme rouge des Tuileries (Paris, published by the author, 22 rue d'Angouleme, 1863)

stops.name: Paris, Histoires heroiques for the Prince Imperial
stops.date_confidence: attested as a title in BnF-linked catalogue data. Month and day are placeholders; the two 1863 books are ordered here by subject, not by any known sequence of issue.
stops.campa: The same year he brings out Histoires heroiques des Francais, racontees a Son Altesse Napoleon-Eugene, prince imperial, addressed to a boy of seven who is heir to the throne. The man who told the Jacobin club in 1848 that he stood in the line of 1793 now writes French heroism for the dynasty's child, nine years after dating a prophecy of that child's birth. The two books of 1863 come out of one desk in one season. The boy they are addressed to is seven years old.
suggested_refs: Histoires heroiques des Francais, racontees a S. A. Napoleon-Eugene, prince imperial (1863)
sources: BnF-linked catalogue data cited in the dossier's sourcing

stops.name: Paris, Le Moniteur catholique
stops.date_confidence: attested; the BnF authority record and periodical listing give him as editor-in-chief or manager of Le Moniteur catholique: journal du jeudi et du dimanche. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He is put at the head of Le Moniteur catholique, journal du jeudi et du dimanche, an openly Catholic paper appearing twice a week, and he edits it while the occult work goes on beside it. Nothing suggests he held the two apart: the Histoire de la magie will set magic inside providence and close on the crown of the mage. He has written for the Jacobins, for the Empire and for the Church, under four names, in the space of seventeen years. He is fifty-four.
stops.quote: Remember, then, son of earth, that man should, like God, act without ceasing. To will nothing and do nothing is more fatal than to will and do ill.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), Arcanum I: The Magus, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw
suggested_refs: Le Moniteur catholique: journal du jeudi et du dimanche (Paris, from 1865)

stops.name: Paris, Fulla l'Egyptienne, signed Charles Moreau
stops.date_confidence: attested; BnF search returns 'Fulla l'egyptienne' (1866), and the BnF authority record carries 'Moreau, Charles (1811-1872)' among his rejected name forms. Older accounts of the pseudonym give it as 'Christian Moreau', which the authority record does not support. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: A novel called Fulla l'Egyptienne comes out over the signature Charles Moreau. The national library's authority file catalogues Moreau, Charles among his rejected name forms, alongside Christian, Paul and Christian, Pierre and Pitois, Jean-Baptiste. Egypt is already in the title four years before the Histoire de la magie takes its readers down beneath the Sphinx. What the novel contains, and whether it rehearses the initiation, has not been established.
suggested_refs: Fulla l'Egyptienne (Paris, 1866), published as by Charles Moreau

stops.name: Paris, the horoscope of Napoleon I, signed Lussides
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the pamphlet Horoscope de Napoleon Ier is signed 'Lussides', and the attribution to Christian is Paul Chacornac's, resting on extensive reuse of language and material from L'Homme rouge des Tuileries. It is treated as strongly probable in modern tarot-historical scholarship and was not verified here against a primary signed copy. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: An astrological pamphlet appears under the name Lussides: Horoscope de Napoleon Ier, casting the nativity of an emperor forty-seven years dead. Paul Chacornac, going through it later, found whole passages carried over from L'Homme rouge des Tuileries and assigned it to Christian. No signed copy has been produced to settle the question. The attribution is treated as probable throughout the later literature and has never been tested against one. Lussides would be the sixth name.
suggested_refs: Horoscope de Napoleon Ier, signed Lussides (1868)
sources: Paul Chacornac's attribution, as treated in Decker, Depaulis and Dummett and the literature descending from them

stops.name: Paris, editor of the Messager du Centre
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; modern tarot-historical scholarship places him as editor of the Messager du Centre in 1869, and no masthead was located in this pass. The paper's seat is a provincial one and this file cannot fix it, so the stop is pinned at the canonical Paris pin for want of a located town. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He is placed as editor of the Messager du Centre, a provincial paper whose town no source names and of which no masthead has been found. He is fifty-eight, and the Empire has eighteen months to live. In the same stretch of years the manuscript of the Histoire de la magie is being finished, six hundred and sixty-six pages of it, and this last of his newspaper posts is what pays while it is written. No number of the paper was located in any listing consulted.

sources: Modern tarot-historical scholarship, reconstruction; primary masthead not located

segments.name: Histoire de la magie: the Initiation That Never Happened

stops.name: Paris, Furne, Jouvet et Cie: six hundred and sixty-six pages
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Wellcome Collection catalogue record gives publisher Furne, Jouvet et cie, place Paris, date 1870, and the physical description viii and 666 pages with frontispiece, illustrations and plates. The archive.org item confirms the seven-book structure. The firm's street address in 1870 is not in the record, so the coordinate is central Paris. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Furne, Jouvet et Cie of Paris publish Histoire de la magie, du monde surnaturel et de la fatalite a travers les temps et les peuples: viii and 666 pages, frontispiece and plates, seven books running from the supernatural in general through the Egyptian mysteries, the oracles, medieval magic, astrology and horoscopy. It is the work everything else he wrote is forgotten for. He is fifty-nine and this is somewhere near the ninetieth volume of his career.
stops.quote: The Science of Will, the principle of all wisdom and source of all power, is contained in twenty-two Arcana or symbolic hieroglyphs, each of whose attributes conceals a certain meaning and which, taken as a whole, compose an absolute doctrine memorised by its correspondence with the Letters of the sacred language and with the Numbers that are connected with these Letters.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), prefatory definition of the 22 Arcana, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw
suggested_refs: Histoire de la magie, du monde surnaturel et de la fatalite (Paris: Furne, Jouvet et Cie, 1870), viii + 666 pp.

stops.name: Paris, the treatise Iamblichus did not write
stops.date_confidence: attested as text: the French sentence was read directly in the digitized original, Livre deuxieme, around p. 106. That the cited passage does not appear in Iamblichus is the finding of Decker, Depaulis and Dummett, who compared the claim against the De mysteriis; that comparison was not independently re-run here. The month is an ordering placeholder inside the publication year.
stops.campa: In Book Two he cites Iamblichus of Chalcis, the fourth-century Neoplatonist, as his authority for the Egyptian initiation: a treatise on the mysteries in which, he writes, the principal scenes of the trials are related. The claim gives an invented ceremony a fourth-century authority. Decker, Depaulis and Dummett later set the passage against the actual text of the De mysteriis and found nothing of the kind in it. In 1870 a Paris reader had no copy of the De mysteriis at hand to check it against.
stops.quote: Jamblique, de Chalcis en Coelé-Syrie, qui vivait dans la première moitié du IVe siècle de notre ère, nous a laissé un traité des mystères égyptiens, dans lequel sont relatées les principales scènes des épreuves de l'initiation.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, Histoire de la magie (Paris, 1870), Livre deuxieme, p. 106; French original read in the archive.org digitization, accents restored from the plain-text transcription
suggested_refs: Iamblichus, De mysteriis Aegyptiorum, the treatise Christian cites and does not quote
sources: Decker, Depaulis and Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards (1996)

stops.name: Giza, the Sphinx: the door he never walks through
stops.date_confidence: literary setting, not a journey; nothing in any source suggests Christian ever travelled to Egypt, and this stop marks a page of the 1870 book rather than a place he stood. The French sentence is verbatim from the digitized original. The date is the publication year and the month is an ordering placeholder.
stops.campa: The Sphinx of Giza, he writes, served as the entrance to the sacred underground where the trials of Magism were undergone. There is no such entrance and there was no such trial. Christian has never seen the Sphinx: he is in Paris, at a desk, writing Egypt out of books he catalogued for the Ministry. No record puts him outside Europe at any point in his life. In his account the candidate goes down beneath the stone at night, alone, carrying a lamp, and is not told what is coming next.
stops.quote: Le Sphinx de Giseh, dit l'auteur du Traité des Mystères, servait d'entrée aux souterrains sacrés dans lesquels étaient subies les épreuves du Magisme.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, Histoire de la magie (Paris, 1870), Livre deuxieme, immediately following the Iamblichus citation; accents restored from the plain-text transcription
suggested_refs: The Great Sphinx of Giza, which has no subterranean initiation chamber
sources: Decker, Depaulis and Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards (1996)

stops.name: Giza, the Great Pyramid: seventy-eight stages and twenty-two images
stops.date_confidence: literary setting, not a journey; Book II of the 1870 volume is titled Les Mysteres des Pyramides, confirmed from the archive.org item record. Christian never went to Egypt. The date orders the segment inside the publication year and carries no other information.
stops.campa: Beneath the pyramid the candidate passes a gallery of twenty-two painted images and, in the full account, seventy-eight stages in all: the exact architecture of the tarot Christian had published seven years earlier at his own expense. The initiation is his deck, walked through. Nothing in Egyptology has found a chamber of images under the Giza plateau, and no Greek or Roman writer describes one. The number came first and the antiquity was built to fit it.
stops.quote: THIS, the supreme Arcanum of Magism, is represented by a garland of golden roses surrounding a star and placed in a circle around which are set at equal distances the heads of a man, a bull, a lion and an eagle.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), Arcanum XXI: The Crown of the Mage, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw
suggested_refs: Book II of the Histoire de la magie, 'Les Mysteres des Pyramides'
sources: Decker, Depaulis and Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards (1996)

stops.name: Paris, Cagliostro before the Philalethes in a year that will not hold
stops.date_confidence: attested as a chronological impossibility; Decker, Depaulis and Dummett identify the scene and set it against Court de Gebelin's death on 12 May 1784, a well-documented date. Cagliostro's own Paris dates for 1785 are taken from cagliostro.journey.json. The month is an ordering placeholder inside the publication year; the narrated setting is Paris, May 1785.
stops.campa: In the same volume Christian stages a scene at the Philalethes convention in Paris, May 1785: Cagliostro interrogated by an assembly of masons, with Antoine Court de Gebelin presiding over the questioning. Cagliostro is in Paris that year and will be arrested there in August over the Diamond Necklace. Christian narrates the exchange as a memoir, with speeches, at length. Court de Gebelin died on 12 May 1784, a year before the meeting Christian seats him at.

stops.name: Paris, lames and arcanes
stops.date_confidence: attested; Decker, Depaulis and Dummett's terminological analysis credits Christian with popularizing lames and arcanes in French occult usage and shows that the paired terms major and minor arcana are not his, appearing later in Ely Star and Papus in the late 1880s. The month is an ordering placeholder inside the publication year.
stops.campa: The vocabulary sets. Lames for the cards, arcanes for what they hold: French occultism takes both from Christian and keeps them. He is working a seam Etteilla opened eighty years before, when the Paris print-seller first sold the tarot as an Egyptian book and dealt it for money, and Court de Gebelin before that. The paired terms major and minor arcana are not his. Ely Star and Papus put those together in the late 1880s. By then Christian is ten years dead.
stops.quote: Human will [I], illuminated by Knowledge [II] and manifested by action [III], creates Realisation [IV] of a power that it can use rightly or wrongly, according to its good and evil Inspiration [V], in the circle described for it by the laws of universal order.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), closing synthesis of the 22 Arcana, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw
suggested_refs: The Grand Tarot Belline, said to carry Christian's 1863 nomenclature forward

segments.name: The Siege, Lyon, and the Catalogue

stops.name: Paris, the two sieges
stops.date_confidence: the two-volume Histoire de la guerre avec la Prusse et des deux sieges de Paris, 1870-1871 is attested in the UPenn bibliography, dated 1872. His personal presence in Paris through the siege is plausible from the subject and his residence but is not separately documented. The stop is dated to the events; month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The Empire falls in September, the Prussians close the ring, and Paris eats its zoo through the winter. In the spring the Commune rises and the second siege is fought by Frenchmen against Frenchmen. Christian, sixty years old, writes it down: Histoire de la guerre avec la Prusse et des deux sieges de Paris, 1870-1871, two volumes, out in 1872. Thirty years earlier he had written the conquest of Algeria for this same state. It is the last substantial history he publishes.
suggested_refs: Histoire de la guerre avec la Prusse et des deux sieges de Paris, 1870-1871, 2 vols. (1872)

stops.name: Paris, the letters to Jacques Charrot
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; letters running February to June to a pupil named Jacques Charrot are reported by Ross Nichols and repeated by later tarot historians as surviving or once accessible. No primary letter was located or fetched in this pass, and the year is given as 1871 in those accounts. The Faculty of Occult Sciences never became a functioning institution.
stops.campa: Letters survive, or survived, running from February to June, to a pupil named Jacques Charrot: onomantic astrology, the reading of a fate out of a name, with Eliphas Levi and the cartomancer Edmond invoked as authorities. He complains of his health. He describes a Faculty of Occult Sciences he means to found, with a curriculum and a body of students. No such faculty ever opened. The letters themselves have not been located by anyone writing about him since Ross Nichols reported them.
stops.quote: for if Arcanum XII appears in your horoscope, violent death will lie in wait for you on your path through life. But if the world makes an attempt upon your earthly life, do not die without accepting with resignation the will of God and without pardoning your enemies
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), Arcanum XII: The Sacrifice, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw; quoted as a verbatim fragment of a longer sentence
suggested_refs: The Charrot correspondence, reported by Ross Nichols and not located since
sources: Ross Nichols and later tarot historians; no primary letters located

stops.name: Paris, the death the catalogue gives him
stops.date_confidence: attested as a record, contradicted as a fact; the BnF authority record, fetched directly, lists 'Christian, P. (1811-1872)' with a death date of 7 December 1872 and gives no place. Every other biographical tradition, including encyclopedia.com and the Lyon genealogical indexing, gives 12 July 1877 at Lyon. The contradiction is flagged and not resolved. The coordinate is the national library, where the record lives.
stops.campa: The authority file of the Bibliotheque nationale de France, which binds roughly one hundred bibliographic records to this one man as author, translator and prefacer, gives his death as 7 December 1872 and lists his rejected names: Pitois, Jean-Baptiste; Christian, Paul; Christian, Pierre; Moreau, Charles. Every other biographical tradition gives 1877, at Lyon. The catalogue has not been corrected, and no source explains where 7 December 1872 came from.

sources: BnF authority record, catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb12327453r, fetched directly

stops.name: Lyon, the marriage in the second arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; a Geneanet genealogical page citing 'Mariages de Lyon 02' gives the marriage to Louise Marie Tortillet (1825-1877) on 26 June 1877, and that page returned 403 Forbidden on direct fetch. The civil act itself was not retrieved. It conflicts with the reported 1853 marriage to an Italian woman; neither is resolved here. Coordinate is the canonical Lyon pin, not the arrondissement mairie.
stops.campa: A civil register of the second arrondissement of Lyon records the marriage of Jean-Baptiste Pitois, sixty-six years old, to Louise Marie Tortillet, fifty-two. The index is a genealogist's transcription; the act itself has not been retrieved, and the page carrying the index refused every request. He is far from the Paris he lived in for forty years, and nothing in any source explains what brought him to Lyon. Sixteen days after the wedding he is dead.
suggested_refs: The civil registers of marriages, Lyon 2e arrondissement, June 1877
sources: gw.geneanet.org/jfriedel, citing 'Mariages de Lyon 02': inaccessible, 403 Forbidden

stops.name: Lyon, death at sixty-six
stops.date_confidence: attested by two independent biographical sources; encyclopedia.com states plainly that he died 12 July 1877 at Lyons, and en.wikipedia gives the same, with the Lyon civil-register indexing agreeing. It contradicts the BnF authority record's 7 December 1872, flagged at the previous stop and not resolved. The death act itself has never been retrieved by anyone writing about him, and no cause, cemetery, or grave has been located in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Jean-Baptiste Pitois dies at Lyon on 12 July 1877, sixty-six years old. No cause is recorded in any source consulted. No cemetery, no stone, no grave has been located, and the death act itself has never been retrieved by anyone who has written about him. He had married two weeks before. The catalogue keeps roughly a hundred entries under five names, and one of those names he took at seventeen in a Trappist novitiate. What is certain of the end is the date and the city.
stops.quote: It is the emblem of destruction and perpetual rebirth of all forms of Being in the domain of Time.
stops.quote_source: Paul Christian, The History and Practice of Magic (1870), Arcanum XIII: The Scythe, trans. James Kirkup and Julian Shaw
suggested_refs: The death act of Jean-Baptiste Pitois, Lyon, 12 July 1877, never retrieved
